title: The borrowed name
summary: Recognize SQL injection and choose evidence that tests the boundary.

scenario.briefing: A search endpoint builds SQL by inserting the user's name into the query text. Review the change and choose tests that would expose the vulnerability.

objectives.description: Choose tests that include hostile input.
Check understanding through the remaining explanation and transfer evidence.

hints: Look at how name is inserted into the SQL string.
A quote in the input can end the string literal and add SQL.
The test suite must include quotes, comments, and a normal case.
Use parameterized queries and test hostile strings such as ' OR '1'='1.

misconceptions.description: Believing input validation alone makes string-built SQL safe.
misconceptions.feedback: Validation helps, but parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL syntax. Accepting the endpoint leaves the query construction unsafe.
Security tests must include hostile strings that try to change the query structure. Reading the function is not a test case.

misconceptions.description: Treating validation as a replacement for parameterized queries.
misconceptions.feedback: Validation can reject some inputs, but only parameter binding keeps every value outside the SQL grammar.

sections.title: Injection changes syntax
sections.body: String interpolation mixes data into command syntax. If a value contains a quote or separator, it can end the intended literal and introduce new SQL. The database executes the resulting text with the application's permissions.

sections.title: Separate data from commands
sections.body: Parameterized queries send SQL structure and values separately, so quotes in data remain data. Test with malicious strings and keep least privilege on the database account. Validation and parameterization solve different parts of the problem.

vocabulary.definition: Untrusted data changing the structure of a command.
A query with placeholders whose values are supplied separately.

steps.title: Review the search endpoint
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.

artifact.title: Customer search
artifact.caption: Submitted as a small internal search feature.

findings.label: User input is interpolated into SQL syntax.
A quote in the name can change the query structure.
A parameterized query would keep the value separate from SQL.
Internal endpoints do not need injection protection.

verdicts.label: Reject until the SQL uses parameters and adversarial tests exist

steps.explanation: Length validation does not make interpolation safe. The value must be bound as a query parameter.
hints: Follow the value of name from the function argument to the SQL text.
Look for a quote character that ends the intended string literal.
Ask what evidence would show the value stays data instead of SQL syntax.
Reject the endpoint: the query needs parameters, and the tests must include hostile strings.

steps.title: Choose adversarial tests
steps.prompt: Select the test inputs you would keep for the search endpoint.

cases.label: ' OR '1'='1 → must not return every customer
'; DROP TABLE customers; -- → must be handled as data
Read the function and decide it looks fine

steps.explanation: A security test suite includes ordinary data, quotes, SQL keywords, and comment syntax. Reading code is not a test.
hints: Start with ordinary input so the search still works.
Add a quote and a boolean expression that tries to match every row.
Add comment syntax and a destructive statement as data.
Keep normal, quote, OR, comment, and empty-string cases; reading the code is not a test.

steps.title: Defense in depth

statements.label: Parameterized queries separate values from SQL structure.
A database account should have only the permissions it needs.
Input validation alone makes interpolation safe.
Hostile input belongs in the test suite.

steps.explanation: Parameterization is the primary defense. Least privilege limits damage, and hostile tests catch regressions.
hints: Separate validation from how the query is built.
Parameter binding keeps values outside the SQL grammar.
Least privilege limits the damage but does not stop injection.
Select parameterization, hostile-input testing, and least privilege; reject the claim that validation alone is enough.
